name: Okinawa / Banting diet

card.summary: A 19th-century low-carbohydrate eating plan (William Banting) paired in forums with the traditional Okinawan diet, both used to lean out and look healthier.
card.note: The Okinawa diet has its own wiki entry.

quick.overview:
William Banting, a London undertaker, published an 1863 pamphlet describing how he lost weight by cutting starch, sugar, beer, milk and butter and eating meat, greens, fruit and dry wine. It is often cited as the first popular low-carbohydrate diet.

The appearance payoff is a leaner body. The Okinawa diet, a traditional plant-forward eating pattern, is grouped here because both are discussed as lifestyle approaches to weight and healthy ageing.
quick.how: Banting described four meals a day built around meat, vegetables and fruit while avoiding starchy and sugary foods. Modern "Banting" diets (popularised in South Africa by Tim Noakes) take the name for high-fat, low-carbohydrate eating.
quick.risks: Individual medical conditions and medicines change what diets suit a person; clinicians advise discussing major diet changes with a doctor. Reviews note that the type of fat, protein and carbohydrate matters more for chronic-disease risk than quantity.

lead: William Banting (c. 1796-1878) was a London undertaker and coffin maker who, once obese, became the first to popularise a weight-loss diet that limited carbohydrates [1]. His 1863 "Letter on Corpulence, Addressed to the Public" described the regimen as a personal testimonial after fasts, spa visits and exercise had failed him [1].

The plan involved four meals daily of meat, greens, fruit and dry wine, and avoided sugar, starch, beer, milk and butter [1]. He reported falling from 202 lb in August 1862 to 156 lb by September 1863 [1]. The suggestion came from physician William Harvey, who had learned of the low-carbohydrate approach used for diabetes from Claude Bernard in Paris [1].

"Banting" became a verb in Victorian England, and in Swedish "banta" still means dieting [1]. Tim Noakes later gave the name to his high-fat, low-carbohydrate diet in South Africa [1]. The Okinawa diet, a traditional Japanese pattern, appears in reviews of diets associated with healthy longevity [2][3].

chain: Cut starch and sugar, eat meat, greens and fruit
Leaner, more defined face and body
angle.text: Banting presented his diet as a way to lose substantial weight. Leaner body composition is how diets like this affect appearance, including how defined the face and jaw look.

paras: Banting's diet restricted starch, sugar, beer, milk and butter and emphasised meat, greens, fruit and dry wine [1].

Banting first self-published the pamphlet and donated profits to charity; later editions were issued in London [1]. "Do you bant?" became a common phrase [1]. Gary Taubes's Good Calories, Bad Calories opens with Banting's story [1].

Okinawa is among the "Blue Zones", long-lived populations studied for diet [3]. A narrative review links traditional patterns including Okinawan with lower mortality [2], while another review cautions that being documented in a long-lived group does not prove diet is the cause and that these diets are not uniform or stable over time [3].
No studies found of the 1863 regimen itself. Broader reviews examine traditional diets and healthy ageing [2][3].

timeline.event: Letter on Corpulence published; weight reported at 156 lb by September [1].
